meta.triageRationale: One story with a clear approach: add a short shared 'smallest complete change' section to prompts the daemon already renders (implement-task.md, renderStandaloneImplementPrompt, the design.story alternatives prompt) plus the tests that pin them. No new subsystem, contract, schema or storage change.

summary.prose: The prompts that tell a model to implement a Task, or to enumerate design alternatives for a Story, now also tell it to prefer the smallest complete change: take the first option that fully works, from not building it at all, through reusing what the codebase already has, to the minimum new code. The 'already in the codebase' step points the model at the insrc analyzer, and the rule keeps insrc's own limits: the Task or LLD is the spec, the Task's named tests are still required, and validation, error handling, data-loss handling and security are never cut. The wording is defined once and used at every prompt site, with credit to Ponytail (MIT) in a third-party notice file at the repository root and in a comment at the source.

hldContextSlice.frameworkSummary: Standalone feature — no parent HLD. Design directly against the repo, grounded on the s1 analyze passes. There are no HLD shared contracts to honour.

boundary.internal: Add a smallest-complete-change ladder to the build and design prompts

api.name: SMALLEST_CHANGE_RULE
api.signature: export const SMALLEST_CHANGE_RULE: string  // new, in src/workflow/runners/scope-prompts.ts

returns.meaning: the build-side rule text, to be placed in an implement prompt as its own section: take the first option that fully works (does it need to exist at all; is it already in this codebase, asking the insrc analyzer 'does the codebase already do X?' through insrc_analyze_step before writing a helper; the standard library or a platform feature; an installed dependency; one line; otherwise the minimum code), be lazy about the solution and never about the change, add nothing nobody asked for, name anything deliberately left out; and the limits: the Task or LLD is the spec, the tests the Task names are still required, and validation at trust boundaries, error handling that prevents data loss, security and accessibility are never cut

postconditions: defined once and interpolated at every build prompt site, so the wording cannot drift
carries the source credit as a comment at the constant, not in the rendered text; the repository's THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md names Ponytail, its link and its MIT licence text

api.name: SMALLEST_SHAPE_RULE
api.signature: export const SMALLEST_SHAPE_RULE: string  // new, in src/workflow/runners/scope-prompts.ts

postconditions: interpolated into the alternatives.enumerate prompt next to ANTI_OVERREACH_RULE

dataModelChanges.details: SMALLEST_CHANGE_RULE and SMALLEST_SHAPE_RULE are added beside ANTI_OVERREACH_RULE in src/workflow/runners/scope-prompts.ts, the existing home of shared prompt fragments. The implement template src/prompts/build/implement-task.md gains a 'The smallest complete change' section with a smallestChangeRule placeholder, filled by renderImplementPrompt the way mergeRule is. renderStandaloneImplementPrompt adds the same section in code before its Definition of done. The design.story alternatives.enumerate prompt adds SMALLEST_SHAPE_RULE. The validate prompts, the review prompts, the steering block and every schema are unchanged. A comment at the constants credits Ponytail (MIT, copyright 2026 DietrichGebert, github.com/DietrichGebert/ponytail) as the source of the ladder, and a new THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md at the repository root credits it too: it names Ponytail, links its repository, says which prompts the ladder was adapted into, and reproduces its MIT licence text with the copyright line. Existing tests that pin the rendered prompts are extended, not loosened.

migration.stateBefore: The implement prompts tell the model to implement exactly the Task or LLD and to keep the edit minimal and matching the surrounding conventions, but give no guidance on choosing the smallest complete way; the design.story alternatives prompt lists its HARD RULES and the scope rule without any preference for reusing what exists or for a smallest alternative (render.ts, implement-task.md, design-story/index.ts and scope-prompts.ts from the s1 bundles).
migration.stateAfter: The implement prompts carry a 'The smallest complete change' section, and the alternatives prompt carries the design counterpart, both with wording defined once beside the existing shared scope rule and keeping insrc's limits (the spec wins, named tests are required, validation, error handling, security and accessibility are never cut). Everything else renders as before. The repository also carries a third-party notice crediting Ponytail.

migrationSteps.action: Add the two rule texts to the shared prompt-fragment module, with the credit to Ponytail (MIT) as a comment, and add THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md at the repository root with the credit, the link and the MIT licence text
Add the section and its placeholder to the implement template and fill it in the plan-driven renderer; add the same section to the standalone renderer
Add the design rule to the alternatives prompt next to the scope rule

Extend the prompt tests: the section and no leftover placeholder in every implement prompt, the rule's key phrases and limits, the unchanged sections, the alternatives prompt, and that each site references the shared constants

migration.backwardCompat: Additive text in prompts the daemon renders; no tool schema, IPC, artifact format or setting changes. The new wording reaches users only after the daemon is updated; until then the prompts are as they are. Removing the section and the two constants restores the old prompts.

alternativesConsidered.name: Two shared rule texts, one for building and one for designing
alternativesConsidered.oneLineSummary: Define the ladder once as exported constants beside the existing shared prompt fragment, and interpolate them at every prompt site.
alternativesConsidered.approach: Add two exported strings to src/workflow/runners/scope-prompts.ts, where ANTI_OVERREACH_RULE already lives. SMALLEST_CHANGE_RULE is the build ladder: take the first option that fully works (does it need to exist, is it already in the codebase, the standard library or a platform feature, an installed dependency, one line, otherwise the minimum), be lazy about the solution and never about the change, and never cut validation at trust boundaries, error handling that prevents data loss, security or accessibility. Its 'already in the codebase' rung tells the implementer to ask the insrc analyzer (insrc_analyze_step) 'does the codebase already do X?' before writing a helper. The text states that the Task or LLD is the spec and that the named tests of the Task are still required. SMALLEST_SHAPE_RULE is the design counterpart for alternatives.enumerate: reuse what exists, one alternative is the smallest that fully meets the Story, nothing nobody asked for. The build text is filled into the implement template through a new placeholder and added as a section in renderStandaloneImplementPrompt; the design text is added to the alternatives.enumerate prompt next to ANTI_OVERREACH_RULE. A comment at the constants credits Ponytail (MIT, copyright 2026 DietrichGebert) with its link. Tests extend the existing prompt tests.
pros: One wording per concern, defined once like ANTI_OVERREACH_RULE, so the three build prompts and the design prompt cannot drift
Small: two constants, one template placeholder, two prompt edits, and tests that follow existing patterns
Nothing external runs and no plugin is installed
cons: Every implement prompt grows by a short section
The rule only steers the model; it does not enforce smallness, which the code review does not check either

alternativesConsidered.name: Build prompts only
alternativesConsidered.oneLineSummary: Add the ladder to the implement prompts and leave the design step as it is.
alternativesConsidered.approach: As a1 for the build side only: SMALLEST_CHANGE_RULE is filled into the implement template and the standalone implement prompt. The design.story alternatives.enumerate prompt is not touched, so alternatives are enumerated as today.
pros: Smallest edit, with no change to the design workflow
The build step is where code is actually written
cons: The design step is where a larger-than-needed shape gets chosen, and the build then has to implement it; the request names both
Leaves the design prompts without the 'reuse what exists' rung
alternativesConsidered.reasonRejected: Smaller, but leaves out the design step the request names.

alternativesConsidered.name: Put it in the steering text the controller reads
alternativesConsidered.oneLineSummary: Add the ladder to the insrc steering block in CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md instead of the daemon's prompts.
alternativesConsidered.approach: Add a short section to src/prompts/steering-block.md, which the daemon refreshes into every registered repo's CLAUDE.md and AGENTS.md, telling the controller to prefer the smallest complete change. The daemon's own prompts are unchanged.
pros: Reaches the controller in every turn, not only the prompts the daemon renders
No code change, only text and its copy test
cons: The steering block is kept deliberately small; this adds weight to every session of every repo
The daemon's implement and design prompts, which are what the request names, would be unchanged
A reply-level rule would also affect non-coding turns
alternativesConsidered.reasonRejected: Does not change the prompts the request names and adds weight to every session.

openQuestions: The Story has no acceptance criteria; ac1-ac5 were derived from its stated need and from the request to credit the source.
The Ponytail credit lives in two places, a comment at the constants and a new THIRD_PARTY_NOTICES.md at the repository root; the README is not changed. Add a README acknowledgement if one is wanted.
The rules only steer the model. Nothing checks that a change is the smallest one, and the code review's four dimensions do not cover it; a lean check in the review is a possible later step.
